Business Marketing B2B Marketing: Definition + Strategies B2B Marketing: Definition + Strategies Written by Coursera Staff • Updated on Nov 6, 2026 Discover B2B marketing, common B2B marketing channels, and how to build your strategy. Key takeaways Business-to-business (B2B) marketing is a type of marketing that businesses use when focusing on promoting goods and services to other businesses rather than to consumers, and it involves strategies such as B2B content marketing, social media marketing, and email marketing. B2B content marketing helps you rank in search engine results, which can increase your visibility with potential customers, and help build trust using various types of content, including explainer videos, educational content regarding industry trends, and customer testimonials. You can build your B2B digital marketing strategy by identifying your brand positioning and how set your brand apart from its competition, describing your target buyers, building your brand voice, and selecting B2B marketing channels. B2B marketing means targeting decision-makers at organizations, typically based on logical motics such as return on investment. Read on to learn more about B2B marketing, including common strategies and how to develop a marketing plan for your business. Afterward, if you want to build foundational marketing skills, consider enrolling in the Google Digital Marketing & E-commerce Professional Certificate . It takes an average of six months to complete at a flexible pace and offers opportunities to learn digital marketing fundamentals, become familiar with spreadsheets, and develop skills in social media marketing, relationship management, and media planning. What is B2B marketing? Business-to-business, or B2B, marketing is the process of promoting products and services to other companies to help them improve their operations. It helps create demand and brand awareness. B2B companies often offer products and services such as software-as-a-service (SaaS), professional services, consulting, manufacturing, and wholesale products.Some B2B companies are large and also offer products directly to consumers. For example, Amazon, Meta, and Apple all blur the lines between the two and require both B2B and business-to-consumer (B2C) marketing. Other real-world examples of B2B companies include: Microsoft Salesforce Mailchimp When selling to other companies, remember that B2B marketing involves considerations and best practices that differ from those associated with marketing to individual consumers (B2C). For example, B2B customers generally look for products and services that will contribute to a healthier bottom line while avoiding investments with a low likelihood of a return. Considering that businesses may be responsible for payroll and other large business expenses, there may be more at stake for B2B than B2C customers, so when marketing, you’d want to bear this difference in mind. Explore other differences in the chart below: B2B B2C What it is Marketing to the decision makers at organizations Marketing to individual consumers Product examples Software, office equipment, and supplies, co-working spaces Food, clothing, electronic devices, books, media subscriptions Service examples Consulting and training, web or graphic design, product distribution, ad campaign management Tutoring, hair styling, health care, home cleaning, car repair Buying motives Logic: What’s the financial ROI of an investment? What’s the expertise level of a service provider? Emotions: Will this product solve a problem or fulfill a desire? Sales cycle Longer sales cycle as decision makers consider the return on investment Shorter sales cycle, especially for impulse purchases Market research focus Firmographics of businesses and psychographics of decision makers Demographics and psychographics of individual consumers 7 common B2B digital marketing strategies B2B marketing strategies, which include B2B-focused content marketing, social media marketing, email marketing, and event marketing, can help connect buyers with products and services using a combination of data and content to achieve results. Discover some common B2B marketing channels , both digital and offline, as well as best practices for promoting your business on these channels to help plan your next steps. B2B content marketing Content marketing , particularly SEO content on your website , is an effective way to reach a target audience of B2B customers. Focused content can build trust with decision-makers, increase your website’s ranking in search engine results, and provide a basis for marketing efforts on other channels. Different types of content that work well for a B2B audience include the following: Thought leadership and educational content on important industry trends and strategies that your target B2B customers can use Videos explaining how your products and services can help B2B customers Webpages explaining your company’s method of prioritizing diversity, equity, and inclusion, and what these efforts mean for your target B2B customer Customer testimonials Read more: How to Develop a Content Strategy: A Step-by-Step Guide B2B social media marketing To attract B2B customers on different social media platforms, adopt practices that are specific to a business-oriented audience, and leverage the power of videos for product demonstrations, tutorials, industry highlights, behind-the-scenes content, case studies, “about us” stories, and business-building strategies. Additional strategies to consider include the following: Tailor your posts to each platform. For example, you could repurpose long-form content into a Tweetable tip, an infographic for Instagram, and an excerpt for LinkedIn. Set up in-platform purchase and subscription options on social media. Algorithms may promote this content to more viewers, as it doesn’t lead users away from the platform. Partner with micro-influencers in your niche (users with 10,000 to 99,999 followers) to gain access to their loyal, targeted followers. B2B podcasting Podcasting can be a great way to reach B2B customers and provide them with informative content in audio format. By discussing topics that help businesses thrive, your podcast can establish you as a B2B thought leader. Topics might include: Leadership strategies Industry news and trends B2B customer success stories E-commerce best practices B2B email marketing Email marketing can be an effective way to build relationships with B2B customers and convert leads (potential customers or prospects) into buyers. Artificial intelligence (AI) tools can help optimize email campaigns, drive increased personalization, and automate content generation directed to specific buyers. Additional email marketing strategies to consider include the following: To build your subscriber base, design a lead-capture landing page that addresses a top-of-mind problem or need for your target B2B customers and promises a solution in the form of a lead magnet, such as a downloadable report or a free video tutorial. Make sure your lead magnet actually provides the solution promised on the landing page and demonstrates how your company can help other businesses operate more smoothly. Divide your subscribers into smaller segments based on their roles within a decision-making unit, the kind of business, where they are in the customer journey, and other factors, so that you can tailor email marketing content accordingly. Include attention-grabbing words in your email subject lines, such as solutions to a problem or product offers, to encourage B2B email subscribers to click. Craft each email message to deliver value and lead subscribers to a purchase decision. Emails can expound upon social media and content marketing pieces, offer exclusive information, invite subscribers to complete a survey, shape future content, and announce new products. B2B event marketing Hosting, attending, and sponsoring events, either in person or online, can increase your brand’s exposure and generate qualified leads. Successful B2B events can take on many forms, including: Workshops, classes, and webinars on topics of interest to your target B2B customers Networking events, exhibitions, and trade shows, where you can build relationships with company decision-makers in your target market and introduce them to your products and services Professional conferences where your target B2B customers can learn new information and network with peers Parties, performances, dinners, and other social events to entertain target B2B customers and offer individualized or VIP experiences B2B marketing word-of-mouth and referrals Loyal and satisfied customers can be a great source of new leads, especially in B2B marketing. When a business recommends your product or service and can quantify a positive outcome, it carries authority. To encourage customers to make thoughtful referrals, you might offer referral bonuses or set up an affiliate program . Paid search Paid search, also known as pay-per-click (PPC) advertising, refers to a strategy that marketers use to leverage search engine results pages (SERPs). Ads typically appear at the top or bottom of a search engine results page (SERP), and when an internet user clicks on an ad, the advertiser pays a fee. This strategy can support your B2B efforts by targeting ads to businesses looking for a specific solution that you can provide. To succeed, you'll need compelling ad copy, strategic keywords (search queries B2B customers use to search the internet), and data-driven insights. Build your B2B digital marketing agency strategy A B2B marketing strategy can have a measurable impact on your business as you expand into new markets for your products and services. Follow the steps below to begin building your B2B marketing strategy, starting with positioning your brand to stand out amongst your competitors. Determine your brand’s positioning. Brand positioning is the combination of factors that differentiate your brand from competitors in the minds of your ideal customers. Clear brand positioning can help you build brand equity and, thus, make your B2B marketing efforts more effective. How will your B2B products and services help businesses succeed better than competitors’ offerings ? What associations, ideas, feelings, and concepts will your brand create in customers’ minds? What will they believe about your products and services? What factors will inspire loyalty in your customers? How to create a B2B marketing agency brand positioning statement Use answers to the above questions to craft a brand positioning statement: [B2B audience] will choose [product/service] to experience [benefits and outcomes], because [B2B audience’s beliefs]. Describe your buyer personas. Create a distinct and detailed buyer persona for each type of business you serve. Start by gathering firmographic data (how different organizations behave) on the kinds of businesses you want to target, as well as psychographic data (how individuals behave) on decision-making units within these businesses, using the prompts below to start. Firmographic data on businesses: How would you describe the industry your target business is a part of, including key players, trends, opportunities, and untapped markets? What kinds of products or services do your target businesses offer? What types of consumers do they serve? How many employees work at these businesses? What’s the average annual revenue? How are these organizations structured in terms of leadership, departments, teams, and individual contributors? Psychographic data on decision-makers: What is the role of each decision-maker within your target businesses, and how will they interact with you during the sales process? What motivates these decision-makers professionally? What inspires them to work in this industry? Develop a brand voice. Your brand’s voice is essential to connecting with customers, personalizing their experience with your B2B products and services, and inspiring their trust in your business solutions. The brand voice will shape how you craft every email, social media caption, video script, piece of long-form content, web copy, and more. When conducting B2B market research, collect insights into the language that company decision-makers use to describe their challenges and goals. Draw from customer language to develop a distinct, empathetic brand voice. Select your B2B marketing channels. While it’s a good practice to build a presence and create customer experiences on multiple channels, don’t feel pressured to be on every channel . Prioritize the channels where your target B2B customers are most likely to engage with your content. Create a seamless omnichannel customer journey to increase loyalty and retention rates. Make sure you tell your full brand story on every channel so that your target B2B customers fully understand your offerings, value proposition, what you stand for, and how to take action. Identify your B2B marketing tactics. Once you’ve selected your marketing channels, your next step is to identify the specific tactics you’ll use to reach your target B2B customers. Four examples of tactics to implement include the following: Offer a freemium service or a trial period so B2B customers can experience the impact of your offerings on their operations. Take an account-based marketing approach by networking with contacts at key business targets, building rapport with them, personalizing the communications, and encouraging sales. Use cause-based marketing to design products and campaigns in collaboration with charitable organizations, demonstrating your business's commitment to creating a better world. Create a more impactful, detailed customer journey for a longer sales cycle. You can do this by delivering content that supports buying decisions and emphasizes the outcomes and benefits your products offer. B2B companies often offer products and services such as software-as-a-service (SaaS), professional services, consulting, manufacturing, and wholesale products.Some B2B companies are large and also offer products directly to consumers. For example, Amazon, Meta, and Apple all blur the lines between the two and require both B2B and business-to-consumer (B2C) marketing. Other real-world examples of B2B companies include: Microsoft Salesforce Mailchimp When selling to other companies, remember that B2B marketing involves considerations and best practices that differ from those associated with marketing to individual consumers (B2C). For example, B2B customers generally look for products and services that will contribute to a healthier bottom line while avoiding investments with a low likelihood of a return. Considering that businesses may be responsible for payroll and other large business expenses, there may be more at stake for B2B than B2C customers, so when marketing, you’d want to bear this difference in mind. What’s the expertise level of a service provider? Emotions: Will this product solve a problem or fulfill a desire? Different types of content that work well for a B2B audience include the following: Thought leadership and educational content on important industry trends and strategies that your target B2B customers can use Videos explaining how your products and services can help B2B customers Webpages explaining your company’s method of prioritizing diversity, equity, and inclusion, and what these efforts mean for your target B2B customer Customer testimonials Read more: How to Develop a Content Strategy: A Step-by-Step Guide B2B social media marketing To attract B2B customers on different social media platforms, adopt practices that are specific to a business-oriented audience, and leverage the power of videos for product demonstrations, tutorials, industry highlights, behind-the-scenes content, case studies, “about us” stories, and business-building strategies. Additional strategies to consider include the following: Tailor your posts to each platform. For example, you could repurpose long-form content into a Tweetable tip, an infographic for Instagram, and an excerpt for LinkedIn. What will they believe about your products and services? What factors will inspire loyalty in your customers? Your brand’s voice is essential to connecting with customers, personalizing their experience with your B2B products and services, and inspiring their trust in your business solutions. The brand voice will shape how you craft every email, social media caption, video script, piece of long-form content, web copy, and more. When conducting B2B market research, collect insights into the language that company decision-makers use to describe their challenges and goals. Draw from customer language to develop a distinct, empathetic brand voice. Select your B2B marketing channels. While it’s a good practice to build a presence and create customer experiences on multiple channels, don’t feel pressured to be on every channel . Prioritize the channels where your target B2B customers are most likely to engage with your content. Create a seamless omnichannel customer journey to increase loyalty and retention rates. Make sure you tell your full brand story on every channel so that your target B2B customers fully understand your offerings, value proposition, what you stand for, and how to take action. Identify your B2B marketing tactics. Once you’ve selected your marketing channels, your next step is to identify the specific tactics you’ll use to reach your target B2B customers. Four examples of tactics to implement include the following: Offer a freemium service or a trial period so B2B customers can experience the impact of your offerings on their operations. Take an account-based marketing approach by networking with contacts at key business targets, building rapport with them, personalizing the communications, and encouraging sales. Use cause-based marketing to design products and campaigns in collaboration with charitable organizations, demonstrating your business's commitment to creating a better world. Create a more impactful, detailed customer journey for a longer sales cycle. Join now Activity 3K followers Posts Comments No more previous content Brian Burch Brian Burch 2d Report this post Brian Burch shared this Last week, I had a moment like one I remember from May 2012.

In a fantastic coincidence, both involved CNBC.

On Sunday, November 8, I read CNBC’s November 7 story on America’s new no-employee small business owners.

In January 2009 at HP, I predicted the Great Recession would push laid-off professionals into starting companies. I called them The Accidental Entrepreneur. I began studying the cohort. By 2011, HP overtook Dell for #1 in US SMB PCs.

The moment in May 2012 was a presentation of research findings: 305 US businesses, roughly half founded before 2008 and half after. 35% of the newer founders reported leaving their employer because of the recession. 75% expected their revenue to grow more than 10% vs. 39% of the older companies. CNBC reported on my research and used the nickname I had given the cohort: "velociraptors."

In the fall of 2025, I started my company because I recognized a new and important SMB cohort was forming. In September, in the first issue of The SMB Cohort, I made my prediction public.

The Artificial Entrepreneur is forming.

The CNBC story led me to a paper by Dr. Liya Palagashvili, a labor economist at George Mason University’s Mercatus Center. It was published in July, two months before I made my public call. Despite AI agents I had built to find research just like this, I hadn't known it existed.

She split Census business applications into two kinds: those flagged as likely to hire, and everything else. In the industries most exposed to AI, from early 2024 to early 2026:

• Applications with no sign of hiring rose 27%
• Applications flagged as likely to hire fell 6%

In construction and wholesale, her comparison group for limited AI impact, the no-hiring kind was flat.

Then she checked a completely different source: the monthly household survey behind the unemployment rate, which tracks people and their work, not company filings. People self-employed with no employees rose 7.9% in AI-exposed industries and fell 2.1% in the comparison group.

Two independent sources pointing the same way is what separates a signal from an anomaly.

I carried her comparison forward. From January through September 2026, against the same months of 2024, applications without a hiring flag are up 44% in the AI-exposed sectors. The comparison group is up 11%.

I’m not claiming that AI caused this, or that every application becomes a business.
These are leading indicators. The official counts will confirm or refute it, and I will score it in public either way.

But in 2009, I bet a multimillion-dollar marketing budget on less evidence than this.

The Artificial Entrepreneur is forming NOW.

That's the argument of Issue 005 of The SMB Cohort, out this morning.

I've named three crisis-born cohorts of US small business founders:

The Accidental Entrepreneur.  Born of the Great Recession, 2007–2011.  I coined the name at HP in January 2009.

The Airborne Entrepreneur.  Born of the pandemic, 2020–2021.

The Artificial Entrepreneur.  The cohort AI displacement is creating right now.  It's my prediction, not yet a confirmed wave.

The Airborne Entrepreneur arrived with the loudest signal of the three.  Applications to start a business went from 3.5 million in 2019 to 4.4 million in 2020 to 5.4 million in 2021.  I'm predicting it won't last as a cohort of its own.  Those founders don't disappear.  They graduate, by three paths:

Displacement.  Founders who went back to corporate jobs, lose them and found again.

Yearning.  Founders who went back miss running their own shop, and AI makes a second try cheaper.

Upgrade.  Founders who never left rebuild the business around AI.  Probably the largest path, and the hardest to see.

All three end in the same place:  The Artificial Entrepreneur.

That leaves two cohorts to build a strategy around.  The Accidental Entrepreneur, whose oldest founders are now entering The Silver Tsunami.  And The Artificial Entrepreneur, where I registered my prediction on September 11:  five million net new businesses with no employees between the 2024 and 2028 counts.

If you sell to, lend to, advise or buy small businesses, those are two different customers on two different clocks.

Issue 005 carries three predictions about the Airborne graduation that I can be scored on.  If the data says I'm wrong, I'll say so here.

The essay never mentions starting a business.  His own farm example is about people leaving business ownership:  in the 20th century, the country lost millions of farms, and the families who ran them went to work for someone else.

Agencies, consultancies, law firms, accounting firms, staffing firms, call centers: the invoice counts hours, so the business can only grow as fast as its payroll.  That payroll is the moat.  It's what a big firm has that one capable person doesn't.

I call what's happening to it the Melting Moat.  When AI can do part of the billable work, the hours stop requiring the headcount, and the roster stops being the advantage.  One person can sell what used to take a team.

It's the engine behind my prediction of The Artificial Entrepreneur: founders whose companies grow without hiring the way their growth would predict.

The first evidence came from the labor market.  From 2019 to 2025, employment in business services that sell language and paperwork (contact centers, collections, document preparation, temp help) fell a median 14%.  Comparably paid physical work (pest control, landscaping, building services) grew a median 13%.  A business cycle doesn't split that cleanly.  Something is selecting on the content of the work.

But a melting moat only creates Artificial Entrepreneurs if the work and the people land somewhere new, and the first place they land is a business with no employees.  That count has fallen only once since 1997, in 2008.  So on September 10, before Census published 2024, I wrote down my kill switch: if the count didn't rise from 2023 to 2024, the moat wasn't melting into new businesses, and I was wrong.

Census released the 2024 count yesterday.
2023: 30,427,808
2024: 31,985,874
Change: +1,558,066, up 5.1%

The kill switch didn't trip.  The thesis survives its first scored test.

It was a low bar by design: a kill switch, not a victory condition.  Clearing it says nothing yet about AI.

It is the largest one-year increase in number in Census nonemployer data back to 1997, ahead of 2021 and 2022, the surge of The Airborne Entrepreneur, at about 1.33 million each.

I chose 2024 as my baseline because I expected minimal AI influence on it.  It's the starting line for the prediction I registered September 11: five million net new nonemployer businesses between the 2024 and 2028 counts.  Census should publish 2028 around 2030.

Where the growth lands matters more than how big it is.  In 2024, about 12% of the increase landed in professional services and information (excluding film and music).  If the Melting Moat is real, that share should rise.  If the five million turns out to be delivery and ride-hail, I was wrong, and the number should say so.

Home | The SMB Cohort Home | The SMB Cohort 3 Copy LinkedIn Facebook X Brian Burch Brian Burch 1mo Report this post Brian Burch shared this Seven years after birth, startups founded during the Great Recession were 27 percentage points more likely to still be in business than similar startups founded just before or after it. 

They were 64 points ahead on employment growth.

The obvious explanation is the one I believed for years:  Great Recession startups were founded by better business people and necessity made them scrappier.

The evidence says otherwise.  Daniel Bias and Alexander Ljungqvist, writing in the Journal of Financial Economics, studied 3,870 US startups that filed patent applications between 2002 and 2009.  The recession-born startups weren't better to begin with: they had narrower patents and fewer breakthroughs.  And higher unemployment at birth went with worse outcomes, not better, so founder desperation doesn't explain the gap either.

Retention does.  When the outside job market froze, the people who built these companies had nowhere better to go.  Recession-born startups were 22.4 points more likely to keep their founding inventor through the first year, in a world where 38% of founding inventors normally leave.

Necessity wasn't just the mother of invention.  It was the mother of retention.

That matters for every cohort that follows, including the cohort AI displacement is creating right now, which I call The Artificial Entrepreneur.  If the job market decides who stays, then the job market around a new cohort tells you whether it will compound.

In the fall of 2025, I started my company because I recognized a new and important SMB cohort was forming. In September, in the first issue of The SMB Cohort, I made my prediction public.

The Artificial Entrepreneur is forming.

The CNBC story led me to a paper by Dr. Liya Palagashvili, a labor economist at George Mason University’s Mercatus Center. It was published in July, two months before I made my public call. Despite AI agents I had built to find research just like this, I hadn't known it existed.

She split Census business applications into two kinds: those flagged as likely to hire, and everything else. In the industries most exposed to AI, from early 2024 to early 2026:

• Applications with no sign of hiring rose 27%
• Applications flagged as likely to hire fell 6%

In construction and wholesale, her comparison group for limited AI impact, the no-hiring kind was flat.

Then she checked a completely different source: the monthly household survey behind the unemployment rate, which tracks people and their work, not company filings. People self-employed with no employees rose 7.9% in AI-exposed industries and fell 2.1% in the comparison group.

Two independent sources pointing the same way is what separates a signal from an anomaly.

I carried her comparison forward. From January through September 2026, against the same months of 2024, applications without a hiring flag are up 44% in the AI-exposed sectors. The comparison group is up 11%.

I’m not claiming that AI caused this, or that every application becomes a business.
These are leading indicators. The official counts will confirm or refute it, and I will score it in public either way.

But in 2009, I bet a multimillion-dollar marketing budget on less evidence than this.

The Artificial Entrepreneur is forming NOW.

Agencies, consultancies, law firms, accounting firms, staffing firms, call centers: the invoice counts hours, so the business can only grow as fast as its payroll.  That payroll is the moat. It's the engine behind my prediction of The Artificial Entrepreneur: founders whose companies grow without hiring the way their growth would predict.

That count has fallen only once since 1997, in 2008. They were 64 points ahead on employment growth.

The obvious explanation is the one I believed for years:  Great Recession startups were founded by better business people and necessity made them scrappier.

The evidence says otherwise.  Daniel Bias and Alexander Ljungqvist, writing in the Journal of Financial Economics, studied 3,870 US startups that filed patent applications between 2002 and 2009.  The recession-born startups weren't better to begin with: they had narrower patents and fewer breakthroughs.  And higher unemployment at birth went with worse outcomes, not better, so founder desperation doesn't explain the gap either.

Retention does.  When the outside job market froze, the people who built these companies had nowhere better to go.  Recession-born startups were 22.4 points more likely to keep their founding inventor through the first year, in a world where 38% of founding inventors normally leave.

Necessity wasn't just the mother of invention.  It was the mother of retention.

That matters for every cohort that follows, including the cohort AI displacement is creating right now, which I call The Artificial Entrepreneur.  If the job market decides who stays, then the job market around a new cohort tells you whether it will compound.
